abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Over the past decade, ex vivo autologous chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)‐T‐cell therapies have reshaped the treatment of B‐cell malignancies. Despite their remarkable clinical efficacy, their application remains limited by complex manufacturing processes, demanding logistics, long turnaround times, and substantial costs. In vivo CAR approaches are emerging as a potential solution to address these barriers by enabling direct induction of CAR expression in T cells and other immune cells through in‐patient delivery of genetic constructs. This review provides an overview of the current landscape of in vivo CAR therapies. We describe the major delivery platforms under clinical development, with a focus on lentiviral vectors (LVVs) and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), and discuss their distinct features in terms of manufacturing, mechanism of action, safety, therapeutic applications, and optimization strategies. We also summarize ongoing clinical trials exploring in vivo CAR approaches for hematologic malignancies, solid tumors, and autoimmune diseases. Finally, we highlight the key scientific and clinical challenges that remain, and examine strategies under investigation to overcome these limitations and advance in vivo CAR therapies toward broader clinical translation.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)‐T cells have transformed the therapeutic landscape of hematologic malignancies. 1 , 2 Since the first clinical report in 2011, tens of thousands of patients have received CAR‐T‐cell therapy worldwide.3, 4, 5 As of 2026, seven CAR‐T‐cell therapies targeting either CD19 or BCMA have been approved in the United States and Europe for the treatment of B‐cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, B‐cell lymphomas, and multiple myeloma. 6 , 7 , 8 Early clinical data suggest that CAR‐T cells may also have therapeutic potential in autoimmune diseases. 9 , 10 , 11

Despite their remarkable efficacy, CAR‐T cells, often described as “living drugs,” present significant limitations. Conventional CAR‐T‐cell therapy relies on autologous cells manufactured ex vivo, which entails complex logistics, lengthy production times, and high costs. 12 , 13 , 14

To overcome these challenges, efforts are underway to develop “universal” or “off‐the‐shelf” CAR‐T cells. One strategy uses allogeneic CAR‐T cells derived from healthy donors. 15 This approach requires genome editing, such as TRAC and B2M knockout via CRISPR/Cas9 or TALENs, to prevent graft‐versus‐host disease and CAR‐T‐cell rejection. 16 , 17 , 18 However, allogeneic CAR‐T cells face inherent limitations, including complex ex vivo genome engineering, the need for highly immunosuppressive lymphodepletion, and limited persistence in vivo. 15 , 17

Recent technological advances in in vivo gene delivery, exemplified by mRNA–lipid nanoparticle (LNPs) vaccines developed for COVID‐19, have accelerated the exploration of in vivo CAR‐T‐cell approaches. 19 In this review, we discuss the advantages and limitations of in vivo versus ex vivo CAR‐T‐cell therapies. We describe the mechanisms of the two in vivo CAR strategies currently under clinical investigation: lentiviral vectors (LVVs) and LNPs. We then compare these approaches in terms of efficacy, safety, and potential clinical indications. Finally, we summarize ongoing clinical trials and outline future perspectives for in vivo CAR‐T‐cell therapy.

sec.title: HOW IN VIVO CAR‐T CELLS MAY OVERCOME THE LIMITATIONS OF EX VIVO CAR‐T CELLS
sec.p: Despite their remarkable efficacy and established long‐term safety, autologous, ex vivo CAR‐T cells present several limitations. 20 , 21 Their personalized production involves a complex and time‐consuming process (Figure 1). Patient's T cells are first collected via apheresis and shipped to a centralized manufacturing facility. Then, they are transduced with lentiviral or retroviral vectors, allowing stable integration of the CAR genetic sequence, followed by ex vivo expansion. The resulting CAR‐T cells undergo rigorous quality control, including vector copy number assessment, immunophenotyping, and sterility testing. 14 Once validated, the cells are released and shipped back to the treatment center for infusion after the patient receives lymphodepleting chemotherapy. 22 This elaborate and highly personalized process entails heavy logistics, prolonged turnaround times (several weeks), and costs exceeding hundreds of thousands of dollars. 12 , 14

sec.p: In contrast, in vivo CAR‐T cells are generated directly within the patient following administration of LVVs or LNPs (Figure 1). Their composition and mechanism of action are detailed in Figure 2. In vivo CAR‐T cells are “universal”, eliminating the need for patient‐specific cell production and immediately available off‐the‐shelf. Compared with ex vivo approaches, in vivo CAR‐T cells offer simpler logistics and manufacturing, as they bypass apheresis, cell shipping, and ex vivo manipulation. These features could make the therapy more scalable, cost‐effective, and globally accessible. 12 Additionally, they may obviate the need for lymphodepleting chemotherapy and its potential short and long‐term toxicities, including immune effector cell‐associated hematotoxicity (ICAHT) and infectious complications. 23

caption.p: Lentiviral vectors (LVVs) and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) allow in vivo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) expression. Schematic comparison of composition, mechanism of action, and expression kinetics of LVV‐based and LNP‐based in vivo CAR platforms. LVVs deliver CAR‐encoding genetic material that integrates into the host genome, enabling durable CAR expression and long‐term cell persistence after a single administration. In contrast, LNPs deliver CAR‐encoding RNA that is translated in the cytoplasm without genomic integration, resulting in transient CAR expression that typically requires repeat dosing. These distinct kinetic profiles underlie key differences in durability, safety, and clinical use. IRES, internal ribosome entry site; ORF, open reading frame; PEG, polyethylene glycol; ssRNA, single‐stranded RNA; VSV‐G, vesicular stomatitis virus G.

sec.p: However, in vivo CAR‐T‐cell therapy also carries distinct challenges (Figure 1). Clinical experience is very limited, with only a few patients treated to date. 24 , 25 , 26 Potential risks include off‐target transduction (e.g., in non‐T cells and tumor cells, raising concerns of insertional mutagenesis or epitope masking, respectively), accumulation in organs such as the liver, and immune reactions, particularly in patients previously exposed to viral epitopes. 27 , 28 , 29 , 30

sec.title: IN VIVO CAR METHODS AND DELIVERY SYSTEMS
sec.p: LVVs are the gold standard for ex vivo CAR‐T‐cell generation, but their historical use for in vivo delivery has been limited because conventional vectors display broad, non‐selective tropism and raise safety concerns when administered systemically. 31 , 32 LVVs are engineered, replication‐incompetent viruses derived from human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV‐1) and designed to stably deliver genes into both proliferating and resting cells. 33 Production relies on transient transfection of HEK293T cells with different plasmids encoding (i) the CAR transgene under the regulation of a specific promoter, (ii) the structural and enzymatic proteins that form the viral core, and (iii) an envelope glycoprotein, most commonly vesicular stomatitis virus G (VSV‐G), which is widely used to pseudotype LVVs and confers broad cellular tropism through interactions with low‐density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family members. 33 Upon target cell engagement, LVVs undergo envelope‐mediated receptor binding and membrane fusion, which may occur at the plasma membrane or following endocytic uptake in a pH‐dependent manner, depending on the envelope glycoprotein (Figure 2). Subsequently, the viral core is released into the cytoplasm, where reverse transcription of the RNA genome into double‐stranded viral DNA occurs, followed by nuclear import of the pre‐integration complex and semi‐random integration into the host genome. 31 , 33

For in vivo CAR delivery, this intracellular replication‐incompetent lifecycle is preserved; however, the viral envelope must be retargeted to restrict cell entry and avoid the broad tropism conferred by conventional pseudotyping (Table 1). 24 , 27 , 33 This can be achieved by modifying the envelope glycoprotein itself or by displaying additional targeting moieties on the vector surface to guide transduction toward T cells. 24 , 27 , 34 Tropism restriction is further strengthened by the use of lineage‐restricted synthetic or engineered promoters, which help limit CAR expression to the intended immune cell population. 24 , 31 Once LVVs successfully transduce T cells in vivo, they enable stable expression of the CAR, leading to CAR‐T‐cell activation, expansion, and tumor‐cell killing (Figure 2). After antigen clearance, CAR‐T cell numbers usually contract, but long‐term follow‐up studies with ex vivo CARs have shown that CAR‐T cells can remain detectable for many years in responding patients. 7 This ability to support durable CAR‐T‐cell persistence is a key feature of integrating vectors compared with transient approaches. Accordingly, LVV‐based in vivo CAR approaches are generally envisioned as single‐administration therapies, whereas mRNA–LNP platforms would require repeated dosing to sustain CAR expression due to their transient nature.

sec.p: The main safety concern with LVV‐based in vivo CAR approaches is the potential risk of insertional mutagenesis. In the ex vivo CAR‐T setting, very rare cases of vector‐associated T‐cell lymphoproliferation have been reported, including both benign clonal expansions and a single malignant event linked to lentiviral integration within a tumor‐suppressor locus. 29 , 35 , 36 These observations underscore the importance of minimizing off‐target integration. In the in vivo context, this risk is compounded by the inability to perform product‐level genomic quality control and by the possibility that LVVs may transduce non‐T cells, including malignant cells, which may alter tumor biology, promote clonal expansion, or mask target antigens. 37 To mitigate these risks, several safety systems have been incorporated into CAR designs, including the inducible caspase‐9 suicide switch, 38 the RQR8 depletion marker enabling rituximab‐mediated clearance, 39 and truncated epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which allows antibody‐mediated elimination with cetuximab. 40 Together, these considerations highlight a fundamental trade‐off between durability and safety in in vivo CAR‐T‐cell engineering, thereby motivating the exploration of non‐viral delivery platforms such as LNPs for transient CAR expression.

LNPs carrying mRNA, widely used during the COVID‐19 pandemic, are now being developed for in vivo CAR delivery. Their transient expression profile improves safety by avoiding permanent genomic modification (Figure 2). 25 , 41 In addition, this transiency may enable faster immune reconstitution and reduce long‐term toxicity. 42 Because conventional LNPs preferentially accumulate in the liver and are readily taken up by cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, targeted LNPs (tLNPs) are engineered to redirect uptake toward specific immune subsets. This can be achieved through optimization of lipid composition, often complemented by cell‐specific binders, which together influence biodistribution and support delivery to T cells. 41 tLNPs formulations typically include an ionizable lipid, helper lipids, cholesterol, a polyethylene glycol (PEG)–lipid, and the mRNA payload, with surface binders added when additional cell‐type specificity is required. 41 , 43 Their design aims to enhance biodegradability and minimize reactogenicity while maintaining efficient delivery to defined immune subsets. 43 , 44 Compared with integrating viral vectors, LNPs platforms provide highly scalable, cell‐free manufacturing while avoiding the risks associated with genomic integration (Table 1). Production involves controlled mixing of lipid components with in vitro–transcribed (IVT) mRNA, followed by purification and sterile filtration. 44 A key limitation of standard mRNA is its short intracellular half‐life, prompting the development of long‐acting RNA formats. 45 Circular RNA (circRNA) is now entering early clinical evaluation for in vivo CAR applications (Figure 2). 46 , 47 Other RNA technologies, including self‐amplifying RNA (saRNA), are being explored as approaches to extend RNA expression. 48 In parallel, the physical stability of LNPs formulations presents challenges for global distribution, motivating efforts to develop lyophilized mRNA–LNP products and microfluidic systems capable of on‐demand synthesis. 49

In addition to lymphocytes, the intrinsic uptake of LNPs by myeloid cells has enabled the extension of in vivo CAR approaches to this lineage. CAR‐macrophages (CAR‐M) represent an emerging extension of in vivo CAR strategies, particularly for solid tumors. In this context, mRNA–LNP delivery has been preferentially used to program macrophages in vivo, enabling transient CAR expression without genomic integration. While CAR‐M constructs share the antigen‐binding architecture of CAR‐T cells, their intracellular signaling domains are adapted to macrophage biology to promote phagocytosis, immune activation, and tumor‐microenvironment remodeling rather than direct cytotoxic killing. 50 , 51 , 52

sec.title: ENHANCING CELL‐SPECIFIC DELIVERY AND STABILITY OF IN VIVO CAR PARTICLES
sec.p: LVVs and LNPs require dedicated optimization to achieve cell‐type specificity for in vivo CAR delivery. Specificity‐enhancing strategies can be broadly divided into binder‐based and non‐binder–based approaches. The first strategy, which is applicable across vector platforms, relies on surface‐displayed targeting moieties that engage defined cell‐surface receptors. These moieties can include binders directed against lineage‐associated markers, such as CD3, CD5, CD7, CD8, or the αβ T‐cell receptor, 25 , 34 , 41 , 53 as well as targeting modalities that engage costimulatory receptors, through either antibody‐derived binders or engineered ligand–receptor interactions, most prominently explored in LVV‐based systems (e.g., CD80‐CD28 or CD58‐CD2). 27 Targeting moieties can be introduced by chemical conjugation to engineered vectors, particularly LNPs, using established bioconjugation approaches, including click chemistry, maleimide coupling, and PEG–lipid anchoring. 54 For LNP‐based systems, the stability and persistence of surface‐displayed targeting molecules in circulation represent an additional challenge that may affect targeting efficiency and systemic immune interactions. 55

Beyond binders, LVVs offer multiple non‐binder–based strategies to enhance T‐cell specificity and safety. Vector tropism can be modulated through envelope engineering, including mutations of VSV‐G or the use of alternative glycoproteins with altered cell‐entry properties. 24 , 27 A critical additional safety layer is provided by post‐entry restriction, most commonly achieved using lineage‐restricted synthetic promoters to confine CAR expression. 24 , 56 Further vector surface and production‐cell modifications can limit off‐target uptake and immunogenicity, including incorporation of the phagocytosis‐inhibitory ligand CD47 to reduce macrophage clearance and deletion of MHC Class I expression in producer cells to attenuate immune recognition. 24 Together, these strategies allow LVVs to combine permissive entry with highly selective CAR expression in vivo.

In LNP‐based in vivo CAR delivery, specificity is driven mainly by formulation‐dependent biodistribution. Accordingly, LNP composition must be carefully optimized to favor immune cell transfection while limiting preferential uptake by hepatocytes, which otherwise predominates following systemic administration through apolipoprotein E (ApoE) adsorption and LDLR‐mediated uptake. 57 Among LNPs components, the ionizable cationic lipid is essential for endosomal escape and efficient mRNA delivery in vivo, and its chemistry is actively optimized to modulate biodistribution, support immune cell delivery, and minimize innate immune activation to allow repeat dosing. 25 , 41 The encapsulated RNA payload represents a second major lever to enhance stability and expression. Optimization of untranslated regions and coding sequences improves mRNA stability and translation efficiency in specific immune cell types. 41 Increasingly, data‐driven and computational approaches are used to guide mRNA sequence optimization, followed by experimental validation of expression and function. 58 Finally, modern in vitro–transcribed RNAs incorporate established structural features, including modified nucleosides, optimized 5′ cap structures, and poly(A) tails, to reduce innate immune sensing and prolong expression.

sec.title: IN VIVO CAR DEVELOPMENTS AND CLINICAL TRIALS
sec.p: Since the launch of the first in vivo CAR clinical trial in mid‐2023 in Australia by Create Medicines with MT‐302 in solid tumors, a CAR‐M therapy, the clinical landscape has expanded at a remarkable speed. 52 In less than 2 years, more than 15 first‐in‐humans Phase 1 clinical trials have been registered for in vivo CAR platforms (Tables 2 and 3). CAR‐M aside, all current platforms lead to second‐generation CAR expression directed against well‐validated targets, including CD19, CD20, CD22, and BCMA for B‐cell malignancies and autoimmune diseases, where they have largely demonstrated efficacy and safety in ex vivo autologous CAR‐T cells (Tables 2 and 3). In solid tumors, the focus is on CAR‐M targeting antigens such as TROP2, GPC3, and HER2. 72 , 83 The use of these well‐established targets enables optimization of each platform and supports rapid clinical and commercial translation.

sec.title: Initial clinical outcomes and development of LVV‐based in vivo CAR
sec.p: The first clinical evidence reporting that LVV‐based in vivo CAR therapies could achieve antitumor activity was an abstract from Genocury in 2024 (Table 2). It provided the first data on a single patient treated for a diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma who achieved partial remission by Day 35 post‐infusion. 60

However, the first series of patients treated in a first‐in‐human trial were later reported by Wuhan Union Hospital and EsoBiotec, a Belgian biotech company acquired by AstraZeneca (NCT06691685). 24 ESO‐T01 is an LVV platform, derived from their ENaBL platform, engineered to express an anti‐BCMA nanobody CAR in T cells. This LVV is optimized with VSV‐G mutations, CD47 overexpression, B2M (MHC‐I) knockout, a T‐cell‐specific synthetic promoter, and an anti‐TCR VHH (Table 2). 24 Four patients with heavily pre‐treated multiple myeloma received ESO‐T01 at a single dose and achieved a 100% overall response rate. Two of the four patients presented a stringent complete response, and the two others presented a partial response at a 2‐month follow‐up. 24 Immediately after the infusion, all patients developed acute inflammatory reactions within the first day, some of them with hypotension requiring vasopressor support and hypoxemia requiring supplemental oxygen. Three patients developed Grade 3 cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and immune effector cell‐associated‐neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) occurred in one patient. 24 ESO‐T01 showed a cellular kinetic profile comparable to that of autologous CAR‐T products, with a slightly delayed expansion peak occurring between Days 10 and 17. 24

More recently, Kelonia presented preliminary data from the first‐in‐human Phase 1 inMMyCAR study (NCT07075185) in a late‐breaking oral session at the ASH meeting 2025. 26 , 84 Four patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma received a single infusion of KLN‐1010. KLN‐1010 is an LVV originating from Kelonia's iGPS platform, engineered to express a BCMA‐CAR in T cells with a modified VSV‐G fusogen co‐expressed with an anti‐CD3 binder (Table 2). 26 Peak expansion occurred at Day 15 at a level that was comparable to what has been reported with ex vivo CAR‐T cells. CAR‐T cells remained detectable at 3 months post‐infusion. All four patients achieved MRD negativity at 1 month, sustained up to 3 months in the two patients with the longest follow‐up. Toxicity was manageable, with no severe CRS, no ICANS or delayed neurotoxicity, and mild cytopenias. All four patients achieved an objective response according to the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG)'s criteria: one complete response and 3 partial responses (which were still improving over time). 84

Other assets entered first‐in‐human Phase 1 clinical trials in the past year. UB‐VV111 originates from Umoja's VivoVec LVV platform. 56 UB‐VV111 encodes a payload transgene composed of a CD19‐CAR and the rapamycin‐activated cytokine receptor (RACR) system to promote expansion and persistence of transduced T cells in vivo (Table 2). 56 UB‐VV111 additionally incorporates a multidomain fusion protein (CD58, CD80 molecules and anti‐CD3 scFv) to augment T‐cell activation, proliferation, and transduction efficiency, which was validated in non‐human primates (NHPs). 27 In September 2025, UB‐VV111 was granted Fast Track designation from the FDA for the treatment of relapsed or refractory Large B‐cell Lymphoma and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia and is currently being investigated in a Phase 1 clinical trial in CD19+ B‐cell malignancies (NCT06528301).

Developed by Interius and acquired by Gilead Kite, INT2104 is an LVV allowing the expression of a CD20‐CAR in T and NK cells. 34 This tropism is enabled by an anti‐CD7 scFv and the Gen 2.1 Fusogen, made of three substitutions in the VSV‐G protein, blinding it to the LDLR (Table 2). 34 INT2104 showed preclinical activity in both humanized mouse models and cynomolgus macaques, generating CAR‐expressing T and NK cells after intravenous administration. In NHPs, it selectively transduced CD7+ T and NK cells in lymphoid tissues without detectable off‐target CAR expression, supporting precise targeting and a favorable safety profile. 34 A first‐in‐human Phase 1 trial is now assessing the safety of INT2104 in patients with relapsed or refractory B‐cell malignancies (NCT06539338).

sec.title: Initial clinical outcomes and development of mRNA–LNP‐based in vivo CAR
sec.p: Several LNP‐based candidates have also advanced into clinical trials, including MT‐302 and MT‐303, the first in vivo CAR therapies developed for solid tumors by Create Medicines (formerly Myeloid Therapeutics). MT‐302 is an mRNA–LNP targeting macrophages, encoding a TROP2‐scFv fused to a truncated CD89, indicated for patients with advanced or metastatic epithelial tumors (Table 3). 52 , 72 In November 2025, first‐in‐human results of MT‐302 were reported in 27 patients with advanced solid tumors, showing a manageable safety profile, intratumoral CAR+ myeloid cells with T‐cell recruitment, evidence of tumor‐microenvironment remodeling, and early clinical activity, including one confirmed partial response in a breast cancer patient under long‐term repeat dosing (NCT05969041). 72 MT‐303 is also an mRNA–LNP targeting macrophages, encoding a GPC3‐CAR, indicated in advanced or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma. MT‐303 is currently under investigation in a Phase 1 study (NCT06478693). 71 , 85

HN2301 is a CD19‐CAR mRNA anti‐CD8‐LNP developed by MagicRNA (Table 3). 25 In September 2025, early clinical outcomes of five patients from a first‐in‐human Phase 1 were published 25 (NCT06801119). At a 3‐month follow‐up, all five patients showed a decreased systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) activity index 2000. 25 After one injection, the levels of CAR‐T cells peaked at 6 h and returned to baseline after 2–3 days. 25 Treatment was well tolerated with no severe CRS and no ICANS reported. 25

GT801, developed by Grit Biotechnology, is an in vivo CD19‐CAR mRNA–LNP conjugated with a VHH specific of a T‐cell target (Table 3). 77 Very early clinical outcomes presented at the ASH meeting 2025 in four patients with non‐Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) showed a favorable safety profile, the generation of in vivo CAR‐T cells, the feasibility of repeat dosing, and the depletion of B‐cell in the periphery and in tissues. 77

Other LNP‐based candidates currently being explored in Phase 1 include CPTX2309 (Table 3). Capstan Therapeutics, acquired by AbbVie, developed the ionizable lipid L829, which was evaluated in combination with anti‐CD5 antibodies in rats and anti‐CD8 antibodies in mice and NHPs. 41 , 86 Two intravenous injections induced rapid and durable B‐cell depletion lasting approximately 1 month, with CAR expression peaking at 6 h and declining over 72 h, and no notable toxicity reported. 41

sec.title: IN VIVO CAR CURRENT CHALLENGES AND FUTURE DEVELOPMENTS
sec.p: While early clinical studies demonstrate the feasibility and antitumor activity of in vivo CAR therapies, several challenges remain. These include achieving the optimal balance between durability and safety, ensuring efficient and selective immune‐cell targeting, and preserving the fitness and function of in vivo‐engineered cells (Table 4). Multiple preclinical strategies are therefore being explored to address these limitations.

sec.p: Beyond mRNA–LNP platforms, alternative non‐viral delivery systems, including polymer‐based nanoparticles, have been shown to enable targeted in vivo delivery of CAR‐ or TCR‐encoding mRNA to circulating T cells. 87 Additional non‐viral integrating strategies leveraging LNPs to deliver DNA transposons together with RNA‐encoded transposases are being investigated to enable stable CAR integration in vivo, 81 while requiring careful management of insertional safety. Parallel efforts are also exploring localized delivery strategies, including tissue‐restricted administration 27 and bioinstructive implantable or injectable carrier systems designed to program immune cells in situ, to reduce systemic exposure and promote localized immune activity. 88 , 89 Most recently, targeted genome‐editing approaches have emerged that employ a dual‐particle delivery strategy, combining cell‐selective enveloped delivery vehicles (EDVs), 68 carrying Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes with adeno‐associated viral (AAV) donor templates to enable site‐specific CAR knock‐in at the TRAC locus via homology‐directed repair, placing CAR expression under endogenous transcriptional control and potentially improving persistence, potency, and safety. 69 , 90

From a vector design standpoint, there is currently no intrinsic limitation preventing LVVs from incorporating advanced CAR control features already explored in ex vivo CAR‐T cells, including safety switches and drug‐regulated architectures that enable conditional control of CAR activity and proliferation, as exemplified by Umoja's RACR platform. 56 Overall, in vivo CAR development currently appears to be focused on more precise immune‐cell targeting, improved control of expression durability, and safer strategies enabled by site‐specific knock‐in, whereas antigen discovery and CAR construct refinements have so far dominated the ex vivo CAR‐T field and are expected to gain importance as in vivo platforms mature.

The strategies presented in this review depend on the presence of endogenous T cells with sufficient functional capacity to be reprogrammed and to mediate antitumor activity. Consequently, functional impairment resulting from prior treatments or ageing may reduce their therapeutic performance. 91 , 92 Preclinical studies in non‐CAR‐T settings suggest that strategies aimed at enhancing T‐cell fitness, such as transient systemic immune modulation using thymus‐derived factors encoded by mRNAs, may help mitigate age‐associated immune deficits. 93 Although not yet evaluated in the context of in vivo CAR‐T cells, such approaches could conceptually be leveraged to improve the efficacy of these therapies.

Finally, in vivo CAR‐T therapies will likely compete with bispecific antibodies, which offer off‐the‐shelf immune redirection of in vivo T cells. 94 Compared with bispecific antibodies, in vivo CAR‐T may provide greater functional persistence, while avoiding the individualized manufacturing required for ex vivo CAR‐T cells. However, this potential advantage must be weighed against the relative maturity, controllability, and clinical experience of bispecific antibodies, which currently represent a more established therapeutic modality. Ultimately, it remains to be determined how these differences will translate into clinical benefit as the field continues to evolve.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: In vivo CAR‐T‐cell therapies are emerging as a transformative evolution of cellular immunotherapy. By enabling direct genetic engineering of immune cells within the patient, these approaches offer the prospect of simplified logistics, reduced manufacturing constraints, and global accessibility compared with conventional ex vivo CAR‐T cells. Early clinical data from both LVV‐ and LNP‐based platforms demonstrate that in vivo CAR‐T cells can expand and mediate antitumor activity while maintaining manageable safety profiles.

Viral and non‐viral in vivo CAR technologies, however, present distinct trade‐offs. LVVs offer stable genomic integration, robust expansion, and long‐term persistence, but carry risks of insertional mutagenesis and require highly selective targeting to avoid off‐target transduction. In contrast, LNP platforms provide safer, transient expression with no genomic integration and highly scalable manufacturing, though they may require repeat dosing and still face challenges in efficient, cell‐specific delivery. These complementary strengths highlight that no single platform is universally optimal, and that indications may ultimately be matched to the technology best suited to their biological requirements.

Despite these encouraging results, important challenges remain, including the need to optimize cell‐specific targeting, enhance delivery efficiency, ensure safety, and achieve durable persistence where required. Continued advances in vector engineering, RNA technologies, and cell‐selective tropism are rapidly expanding the therapeutic potential of in vivo CAR platforms. As the field moves forward, in vivo CAR therapies may not only broaden access to established CAR‐T‐cell indications but also open the door to treating a wider range of diseases, including autoimmune disorders and solid tumors, ultimately reshaping the future of gene and cell therapy.
